svg.aria-label: Diagram: the anatomy of a resource declaration showing type as provider plus resource type and apiVersion as a pinned contract, and the lifecycle in which a provider ships new API versions while a template stays on the one it was written against
svg.title: Resource type and API version: what a template actually pins
svg.text: Two strings decide what your template is talking to
One names the thing. The other names the contract you are speaking to it through — and only one of them is obviously a version.
"type": "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts",
type is the resource provider namespace plus the resource type. apiVersion is the version of that provider's
REST API you are calling. Both are required on every resource, and neither has a default.
What the provider does
Ships a new API version whenever it adds
features. Old versions keep working, so the
list of valid versions for one type grows into
a long history you can still deploy against.
What your template does
Stays exactly where you left it. A template
written in 2023 still deploys through the 2023
contract in 2026 — which is the point, and
also why new properties silently do nothing.
Microsoft's guidance, which is the opposite of the usual instinct
Set the latest version when you write the template. Then keep using it: staying put minimises the risk of a new
version changing how the template behaves. Update only when you want a feature a later version introduced.
So apiVersion is not a dependency to keep current. It is a contract to change deliberately — and the failure it
produces when wrong, NoRegisteredProviderFound, names the location and version but not which of them is at fault.
